claims.text: Stability against phase segregation and chemical decomposition in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by the state of nanocrystalline grain boundaries.
Local elastic strain at nanocrystalline grain boundaries can induce partial amorphization.
Strain-induced amorphization produces intergranular amorphous buffer layers.
Intergranular amorphous layers reduce atomic mobility across grain boundaries.
Reduced grain-boundary atomic mobility kinetically inhibits elemental segregation.
Inhibiting elemental segregation preserves the single-phase state and enhances chemical and structural stability.
High configurational entropy maintains the amorphous interfacial state under thermal stress.
A single-phase, nanometer-grained high-entropy alloy with uniformly distributed elements is the intended initial material state.
Controlled mechanical pre-straining is expected to promote formation of amorphous grain-boundary buffers.
Temperatures above approximately 600 degrees Celsius are within the predicted operating regime.
Pre-strained samples will exhibit less grain growth than unstrained samples during otherwise identical high-temperature cycling.
Pre-strained samples will exhibit delayed phase segregation and less chemical inhomogeneity than unstrained samples.
The prediction is expected to apply to high-entropy nanoalloys with grain sizes below 50 nm.
The prediction is bounded to temperatures that activate diffusion but remain below bulk melting.
Oxidation and other environmental reactions may change the predicted behavior.
Chemical clustering can occur over a wide temperature range in at least one Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy system.
High-entropy alloys are not necessarily single solid solutions, and commonly used empirical rules may not reliably identify phase stability.
The strain threshold required to produce amorphous grain-boundary buffers and the magnitude of their long-term stabilization effect are undetermined.
